name: ui-layout
description: Standard for how screens are laid out, in any project. Covers what goes on a screen, order and grouping, primary actions, cards, spacing, type sizes, responsive layout, and patterns for forms, settings, lists, dashboards, empty states, tool pages and landing pages. Load it before building a screen or changing a screen's structure. The ui-text skill covers the words.

# UI layout

A screen has one job. People scan it for the thing they came to do, and every extra box, tile and button competes with that thing. So decide what the screen is for before writing markup, show only what serves that job, and put it where the eye lands first. If a layout needs explaining, fix the layout.

## Where it applies

Every screen someone uses outside of development: public pages, client portals, app screens, admin and internal tools, and personal tools. Hidden developer and diagnostic views are the only exception. Waive their flags with the reason "developer view".

A project's own design system, grid or component library wins over this skill. This skill fills the gaps.

## Plan first

Before writing markup for a new screen, write a short plan in your reply:

- **Job:** what the user comes here to do, in one line.
- **Primary action:** the one action that does that job.
- **Sections:** in order of use, most needed first.
- **Cut:** what you left out, and where it went instead: a help link, a details view, a developer view, or nowhere.

Edits that keep an existing screen's structure don't need a plan.

## What goes on the screen

- Show what users need for the job. Move what they rarely need behind one clearly labeled control, such as a disclosure, a tab or a details page, at most 2 levels deep. Cut the rest.
- No stat tiles or big numbers unless the screen's job is monitoring. On a monitoring screen, every number gets context, such as a target, a prior period or a trend, and no tile repeats a table on the same screen.
- Show each fact once. Don't repeat the page title in a card title, a count in both a tile and a table, or a command in two places.
- System internals go in a developer view: a separate route or a hidden toggle. That covers logs, timings, pipeline or model status and "written by" stamps. Never give them a pane on the user's screen.
- No decoration standing in for hierarchy: gradients, glows, fake browser chrome, decorative badges or emoji icons.

## Order and grouping

- Put the main task at the top and on the leading side. Supporting content goes below it or in a side pane.
- Order sections by how often and how soon users need them, never by the order you built them.
- Lead with the answer or the current state. Details come after.
- Group with space first. Related items sit close together, and the gap between groups is at least one step larger on the spacing scale than the gaps inside them.
- A heading sits closer to its own content than to the content above it.
- Put each control next to what it changes. A filter sits above the list it filters, a row's actions sit in the row, and Save sits at the end of the form it saves.
- Keep the DOM order the same as the visual order, so keyboard and screen reader order make sense (WCAG 1.3.2, 2.4.3).
- Keep repeated navigation in the same place and order on every page (WCAG 3.2.3).

## Cards and containers

- No cards by default. Separate sections with space and a heading, and a divider at most.
- Use cards only for a collection of mixed items people browse, or when the project's design system is card-based.
- Never put a card inside a card.
- Never put a card around a single control or a single line.
- Show items of one kind as a list or a table, not a grid of cards. Lists are faster to scan, compare and sort.
- A box with a border, a shadow, or a fill with rounded corners counts as a card. So does anything named card, panel, tile or box.

## Primary actions

- One primary action per view, plus one in each dialog or side panel.
- Make it the only filled button in its view. Secondary actions are outlined or plain buttons, and tertiary actions are links. Keep at most 3 secondary actions in view and put the rest in an overflow menu.
- On a page, align the primary action with the content's left edge, such as under the last field of a form. In a dialog, put it at the trailing edge with Cancel before it. A project's design system wins on placement.
- A destructive action is never a page's primary action. In a confirmation dialog, the destructive button may be the filled one.
- Never style row actions in a table or list as primary.

## Visual weight

- One focal point per screen: the content or action the screen is for. At most 2 large elements.
- At most 4 font sizes and 2 weights per screen. Build hierarchy with size, weight and color contrast, not with boxes.
- Blur the screenshot or squint at it. The element the screen is for should still stand out first.

## Spacing, alignment and size

- Take every margin, padding and gap from one scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48 or 64px. If the project defines its own spacing tokens, use those. 0, 1 and 2px are fine for hairlines.
- Align content to one left edge. Center only short empty states and dialogs.
- Keep running text near 70 characters wide. That's about `max-width: 60ch`, since a `ch` is the width of a zero and most letters are narrower.
- Forms use one column, labels above fields, and fields as wide as their expected input.
- Click targets are at least 24 by 24px (WCAG 2.5.8), and 44px on touch screens.
- Use one density per page.

## Screen patterns

- **Form.** One column. For a long flow, one topic per page. The submit button names its action and sits under the last field on the left, with a weaker Cancel. No Reset button.
- **Settings.** Sections with a heading, separated by space or a divider. On wide screens, put the section heading in a narrow left column and its controls in a wider right column; stack them on narrow screens. Save at the end, or save each control as it changes.
- **List and detail.** A list or table of items, where selecting one opens its detail. Show two panes from about 840px wide, and separate pages below that.
- **Dashboard.** Only when the job is monitoring. It fits one screen, with the key metric at the top left and context for every number. Prefer bars and lines to gauges, pies and 3D.
- **Empty state.** Replaces the region it fills, with no table headers. Says what's missing and offers one action.
- **Tool page.** Inputs on the leading side or the top, the result on the other side, both visible at once. On narrow screens, the result goes below the inputs.
- **Landing page.** One message and one primary call to action. No pill badge above the headline, no uppercase labels above every heading, no grid of identical icon, heading and text cards, no row of stats, no gradient text, and the same call-to-action band at most once.

## Responsive

- Lay out for 320px wide first. Nothing scrolls sideways at 320px (WCAG 1.4.10). Wide tables and code get their own scroll box.
- Use one pane below 600px wide.
- Every function stays available at every width.
- Recheck grouping after things stack. A label must still sit next to its field.

## Render to check

`ui-standards render FILE|URL` opens the page in headless Chrome. It saves screenshots at 1280 and 375px wide and checks the layout at 320px. For an app that needs a dev server, pass its URL.

Render when:

- You built a new screen or changed a screen's structure. Render before calling the work done.
- Many pages share a template. Render one page of each kind, not every page.

Skip it for text-only edits, small style tweaks, and work where the user's goal doesn't involve how the screen looks.

After a render, look at both screenshots. Does the eye land on the screen's job first? Is there one primary action? Does anything look boxed, crowded or repeated?

## Checker

ui-layout uses the checker in the ui-text skill's folder, `../ui-text/bin/ui-standards` from this skill's folder. It checks HTML, Vue, Svelte, JSX/TSX, CSS, Dart and Swift. Blocking rules stop the end of the turn once, like ui-text flags. Advice appears after the edit and never blocks.

| Rule | Tier | Flags |
|---|---|---|
| `nested-card` | Blocks | A card inside a card |
| `single-control-card` | Blocks | A card around a single control or a single line |
| `multiple-primary` | Blocks in HTML, advice in components | More than one primary-styled action in a view |
| `off-scale-spacing` | Blocks | A margin, padding or gap off the spacing scale |
| `heading-skip` | Blocks | A skipped heading level, or more than one h1 in a view |
| `overflow-x` | Blocks (render) | The page scrolls sideways at 320px |
| `text-overlap` | Blocks (render) | Text overlapping other text |
| `hidden-visible` | Blocks (render) | An element marked hidden that still shows |
| `stat-tiles` | Advice | A row of stat tiles or big numbers |
| `card-grid` | Advice | 3 or more identical cards with an icon, heading and text |
| `type-scale` | Advice | More than 4 font sizes or 2 font weights |
| `deep-nesting` | Advice | Elements nested more than 8 levels deep |
| `badge-above-h1`, `eyebrow`, `emoji-icon`, `gradient-text`, `accent-stripe`, `repeated-cta` | Advice | Landing-page habits |
| `small-target` | Advice (render) | A click target under 24px with no clear space around it |
| `long-lines` | Advice (render) | Text lines over 80 characters |

Static checks see only the markup in the file. A component file isn't a whole view, so its primary-action and h1 counts are advice. Markup built at runtime is invisible to them; a render sees it.

Commands:

- `ui-standards render FILE|URL [--out DIR] [--wait MS]` renders and checks a page. Screenshots go to `.ui-standards/render` in the current folder, which git ignores, unless you pass `--out`. It needs Chrome or Chromium; without one it says so and skips.
- `ui-standards check PATH...` checks whole files or folders for text and layout.
- `ui-standards flags` and `ui-standards waive ID [ID...] --reason "..."` work as in ui-text. List every waiver in your closing message.

A layout can pass every check and still bury the main task. The rules above still apply.

# UI text

People scan screens. They read control labels first, read other text only when they think they need it, and stop reading once they know what to do. So a screen names things and actions. It doesn't explain itself. If a screen needs an explanation of how it works, fix the screen.

## Where it applies

Applies to anything a user of the product sees: web and app screens, tool and dashboard pages, CLI prompts and errors, notifications, emails the product sends, and API error messages that reach users.

Doesn't apply to docs, READMEs, explainer pages, articles or chat replies. Those are prose. A help panel or help page inside an app is prose too. Prose style rules, such as plain-language standards or edits that add voice, never apply to UI text.

A project's own content guide, design system wording or term list wins over this skill. This skill fills the gaps.

## Procedure

1. Before writing code for a screen, list every string it will show, each with its element type and limit.
2. For each string, ask whether the user needs it to act right now. If not, cut it. If they need it only sometimes, it goes in help or a tooltip.
3. Check the list against the rules below. Then write the code.
4. Fix whatever the checker flags.

| Element | Limit |
|---|---|
| Button, menu item, tab | 1 to 4 words. Verb first for actions |
| Field label, column header, heading, legend | 1 to 4 words. A noun phrase |
| Heading or label phrased as a question | Up to 8 words: "Where do you live?" |
| Field hint | One short line, only when the format isn't obvious |
| Error, toast, banner, empty state | 12 words or fewer. One idea |
| Supporting text under a heading | Usually none |

## Rules

### Name things and actions

- Buttons say what happens, as a verb plus an object: "Delete file", "Place order", "Send invite". Never "OK", "Submit", "Yes" or "No" as an action.
- When the object is obvious from context, the verb alone is fine: "Save", "Cancel".
- Labels name the field. They don't instruct: "Email:", not "Enter your email". Never start a label with Enter, Type, Select or Choose.
- Headings name the topic: "Notifications", not "Here you can manage notifications".
- Put the words that matter first.
- One name per thing, everywhere. Don't switch between "project", "workspace" and "space" for the same object.
- Use the words users use, not the system's: "Notifications", not "Webhook config".
- Word a list of options the same way, and move shared words into the group label.
- Every icon-only control gets a visible text label. A tooltip alone isn't enough.
- Show state as state: a chip, a count, a timestamp, a progress bar. "Running, 3 min left", not "The build is currently running and should finish soon".

### Keep off the screen

- How the system works, why it was built, what happens behind the scenes.
- Restating what the layout already shows: "Below is a list of your files".
- Filler: "simply", "just", "in order to", "please", "please note".
- Welcome and thank-you lines. "Thank you for your order" becomes "Order placed".
- Sections called "How it works" or "Under the hood". Diagnostics belong in a developer view, not the product UI.

### Mechanics

- Sentence case everywhere: "Create project", not "Create Project". Proper nouns keep their capitals.
- A colon after a field or group label that sits outside its control: "Email:". No colon on headings, buttons, checkbox labels or tabs.
- A fragment standing alone gets no period: "Changes saved". A full sentence gets one. When a message has two parts, each ends with a period: "Couldn't save changes. Check your connection."
- System errors have no subject: "Couldn't save changes", not "You entered an invalid date" or "We couldn't save". Never make "you" the cause. Use "we" only when real people will act: "We'll email you within 2 days".
- Contractions are fine ("can't", "don't"), except in warnings and destructive confirmations. There, write "do not" and "cannot" so a missed "not" can't flip the meaning.
- Mark optional fields with "(optional)" after the label: "Phone (optional):". No asterisks.
- Tone is neutral. Light warmth only in rare success messages and empty states. No humor and no "Oops" in errors, warnings or messages people see often.

### Defaults where the guides differ

- No placeholder text in fields. Format help goes in a hint that stays visible. A search field may use a placeholder if it has a label for screen readers.
- No ellipsis on buttons that open a dialog. Use "…" for progress ("Saving…") and truncated text. Native desktop menus follow their platform.
- "Close" dismisses a view with nothing to commit. "Cancel" discards. "OK" only acknowledges a message. "Done" only finishes a multi-step flow.
- "Continue", not "Next".
- Drop the pronoun when you can: "Account", "Files". Use "your" if you need one. "I" and "my" only in consent checkboxes: "I agree to the terms".
- "Sorry" only for data loss or an outage the product caused. "Thanks" only after the user did the product a favor, such as sending feedback.
- "Select", not "click" or "tap", except in help written for one platform.
- Numerals: "3 files", "1 error". Don't start a sentence with a numeral.
- No exclamation points. One is allowed for a rare milestone, never in an error.
- "and", not "&".
- "Sign in" and "Sign out", not "Log in".
- When text names a control, use its exact label with no quotes, in bold where formatting exists: Select **Export**.
- Dates and times come from the locale formatter (`Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `DateFormatter`, `DateFormat`), never a hand-written format. Recent events can use relative time: "2 min ago".
- No em dashes. Split the sentence.

## Screen states

- **Empty.** Say what's missing and give the action that fills it: "No messages yet" with a **New message** button. Don't explain what messages are.
- **Loading.** Name what's loading: "Loading calendar…". For waits over a few seconds, show progress or the current step. Never "Please wait while we…".
- **Field error.** State the fix, next to the field: "Use at least 8 characters", "Date must be in the past".
- **System error.** Say what failed and give the next step, as a button where possible: "Couldn't save changes" with **Try again**. Name the cause when it's known: "File is over 25 MB".
- **Success.** Object first, past tense: "Invite sent", "Changes saved". Toasts disappear, so never put the only copy of important information in one.
- **Confirmation.** Ask the specific question and label both choices by their action: "Delete 3 events?" with **Delete events** and **Cancel**. State the consequence only if it isn't obvious: "This cannot be undone." Never "Are you sure?".
- **Disabled control.** Show what's missing next to it ("Select a file"), not a paragraph about why it's disabled.

## Text accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA)

- Every control has a programmatic label: `<label for>`, `aria-label`, `accessibilityLabel`, `semanticsLabel`. (1.3.1, 4.1.2)
- The accessible name contains the visible label and starts with it. (2.5.3)
- Link text makes sense alone: "Privacy policy", not "Click here" or "Read more". Repeated "Change" links get hidden text that names what they change. (2.4.4)
- Headings and labels describe their topic or purpose. (2.4.6)
- Never point to things by color, shape or position alone, like "the green button" or "the menu on the left". (1.3.3, 1.4.1)
- Alt text on a functional image says what it does ("Search"). Decorative images get empty alt.
- Errors are tied to their field (`aria-describedby`) and announced. (3.3.1)

## CLI and API text

- An error says what failed, where, and the fix: `config.yaml line 12: expected a value`. Then the command that fixes it, if there is one: `Run: app init`.
- No banners, taglines or paragraphs on startup. Progress is state: `Uploading 3/12`.
- A prompt ends with the expected input: `Overwrite build/? [y/N]`.
- API error messages a user may see follow the error rules. Codes and details go in other fields.

## Before and after

| Domain | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Settings | Heading "Here you can manage how and when you receive notifications" | "Notifications" |
| Settings | "Your Account Settings" | "Account" |
| Settings | Options "Send me an email when someone comments", "Send me an email when someone mentions me" | Group label "Email me when someone:", options "Comments", "Mentions me" |
| Settings | Toast "Your changes have been saved successfully!" | "Changes saved" |
| Checkout | Button "Submit" | "Place order" |
| Checkout | "Phone number *" with a "* required" legend | "Phone (optional):", required fields unmarked |
| Checkout | "Thank you for your order!" | "Order placed" |
| Checkout | Field error "Invalid card number" | "Card number must be 16 digits" |
| Sign-in | Label "Please enter your email address" | "Email:" |
| Sign-in | "Log In" | "Sign in" |
| Sign-in | "Oops! You entered the wrong password." | "Wrong password. Try again or reset it." |
| Files | "Are you sure?" with Yes and No | "Delete 3 files?" with **Delete files** and **Cancel** |
| Files | "It looks like this folder is empty. Files you upload will appear here." | "No files" with **Upload files** |
| Files | "We couldn't find anything matching your search. Try using different keywords." | `No results for "budget"` with **Clear search** |
| Email | Icon-only trash button | Trash icon with "Delete" |
| Email | "Click here to see older messages" | "Older messages" |
| Calendar | "Please wait while we load your calendar..." | "Loading calendar…" |
| Calendar | "This event repeats every week on Monday" | "Weekly on Monday" |
| Dev tool | "The build is currently running and should be finished in about 3 minutes." | Chip "Running" and "3 min left" |
| Dev tool | Paragraph under the title: "This dashboard shows how tickets move through each stage so that you can spot bottlenecks early." | No paragraph. Title "Tickets by stage" |
| Dev tool | `Error: something went wrong` | `config.yaml line 12: expected a value` |
| Any app | A "How it works" section that explains the pipeline | Removed. A **Help** link if users need it |

## Checker

`bin/ui-standards` in this skill's folder is a Python 3 script with no dependencies. It reads HTML, JSX/TSX, Svelte, Vue, Dart and Swift. It also runs the layout rules from the ui-layout skill. Its text rules flag:

| Rule | Flags |
|---|---|
| `long-label` | A button, label, heading, tab or menu item over 4 words, or a question heading over 8 |
| `long-text` | Any other string over 12 words |
| `multi-sentence` | A string with two or more sentences of 5+ words each |
| `phrase` | "you can", "lets you", "allows you", "this page", "this screen", "so that", "how it works", "under the hood", "please", "sorry", "thank you", "thanks for", "click here", "simply", "oops" |
| `generic-button` | A button labeled OK, Submit, Yes or No |
| `instruction-label` | A label or heading that starts with Enter, Type, Select, Choose or Pick |

When hooks are installed (Claude Code and Codex) or the plugin is (opencode):

- **Before the first UI edit in a session**, the edit is refused until this skill and the ui-layout skill are loaded. Load them and send the edit again.
- **After each edit of a UI file**, it checks only the strings you added or changed and reports each flag with an id.
- **At the end of the turn** (Claude Code and Codex), open flags block the stop once. Fix them, or waive the ones that are prose on purpose. If any stay open, list them for the user in your closing message.

Commands, run from this skill's folder or by the full path the hook messages show:

- `bin/ui-standards check PATH... [--ignore-rule RULE] [--only GLOB]` checks whole files or folders.
- `bin/ui-standards flags` lists open flags in the current session.
- `bin/ui-standards waive ID [ID...] --reason "help panel"` waives flags for this session. Waivers are kept outside the repo. List every waiver in your closing message.
- `bin/ui-standards render FILE|URL` renders a page and checks its layout. See the ui-layout skill.
- `bin/ui-standards selftest` runs the cases in `tests/`.

Patterns can't judge meaning, so short narration gets past the checker. The rules above still apply to it.

Without hooks, run `bin/ui-standards check` on the files you changed before you finish.

## Sources

GOV.UK Service Manual, writing for user interfaces. Microsoft Win32 UI text guide and Writing Style Guide. Apple HIG: Writing, Buttons, Alerts. Material 3 content design. Shopify content guidelines. Atlassian content guidelines. Mailchimp content style guide. NN/g: how users read on the web, icon usability, 10 usability heuristics. WCAG 2.2. ISO 9241-110 and ISO 9241-112.

# claude-ui

Coding agents build screens the way they write documents. Headings get a paragraph underneath, buttons describe themselves, and every section lands in its own bordered card, with a row of stat tiles on top and three buttons of equal weight at the bottom. People scan screens instead of reading them: in Nielsen Norman Group's tests, 79% of users scanned a new page, and cutting a site's text by half made it 58% more usable. Extra words and extra boxes both get in the way.

This repo gives the agent two short standards, one for UI text and one for layout, and a checker that runs on every UI file it edits. It works in Claude Code, Codex and opencode.

## What's in it

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `skills/ui-text/SKILL.md` | The text standard: word limits per element, rules, screen states, text accessibility (WCAG 2.2 AA), CLI and API text, and 22 before-and-after pairs |
| `skills/ui-layout/SKILL.md` | The layout standard: a plan before each new screen, what goes on a screen, order and grouping, cards, primary actions, spacing and type, responsive layout, and patterns for forms, settings, lists, dashboards, empty states, tool pages and landing pages |
| `skills/ui-text/bin/ui-standards` | The checker. Python 3.9 or later, no dependencies. Reads HTML, Vue, Svelte, JSX/TSX, CSS, Dart and Swift |
| `.claude-plugin/`, `hooks/hooks.json` | The Claude Code plugin |
| `codex/hooks.json` | Hooks for Codex |
| `opencode/ui-standards.js` | A plugin for opencode |
| `examples/` | Two pages built to both standards. Both pass the checker and the render with 0 flags |

## How it works

With the hooks or the plugin installed:

1. When a session starts, the agent gets a short text rule and a short layout rule (Claude Code and Codex).
2. The agent's first UI edit in a session is refused until it loads both skills. This happens once per session.
3. After each edit of a UI file, the agent gets a list of flags. Only what the edit added or changed is checked, so old files don't bury it in flags.
4. While problems are open, the agent can't end its turn (Claude Code and Codex). The stop is blocked once. The agent fixes them, or waives the ones that are intended and lists the waivers for you.

Layout flags come in two tiers. Problems block the end of the turn like text flags. Advice appears after the edit and never blocks, because those checks are more likely to be wrong.

### Text rules

| Rule | Flags |
|---|---|
| `long-label` | A button, label, heading, tab or menu item over 4 words, or a question heading over 8 |
| `long-text` | Any other string over 12 words |
| `multi-sentence` | A string with two or more sentences of 5 or more words each |
| `phrase` | "you can", "lets you", "allows you", "this page", "this screen", "so that", "how it works", "under the hood", "please", "sorry", "thank you", "thanks for", "click here", "simply", "oops" |
| `generic-button` | A button labeled OK, Submit, Yes or No |
| `instruction-label` | A label or heading that starts with Enter, Type, Select, Choose or Pick |

### Layout rules

| Rule | Tier | Flags |
|---|---|---|
| `nested-card` | Problem | A card inside a card |
| `single-control-card` | Problem | A card around a single control or a single line |
| `multiple-primary` | Problem in HTML, advice in components | More than one primary-styled action in a view |
| `off-scale-spacing` | Problem | A margin, padding or gap that isn't 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48 or 64px, or one of the project's spacing tokens |
| `heading-skip` | Problem | A skipped heading level, or more than one h1 in a view |
| `stat-tiles` | Advice | A row of stat tiles or big numbers |
| `card-grid` | Advice | 3 or more identical cards with an icon, heading and text |
| `type-scale` | Advice | More than 4 font sizes or 2 font weights |
| `deep-nesting` | Advice | Elements nested more than 8 levels deep |
| `badge-above-h1`, `eyebrow`, `emoji-icon`, `gradient-text`, `accent-stripe`, `repeated-cta` | Advice | Landing-page habits |

A card is a box with a border, a shadow, or a fill with rounded corners, or anything named card, panel, tile or box. A primary action is a button or link with `primary` in its class or variant, `variant="filled"`, `variant="solid"`, SwiftUI `.borderedProminent` or Flutter `FilledButton`. A component file isn't a whole view, so its primary-action and h1 counts are advice only.

Patterns can't judge meaning or purpose, so short narration and a layout that buries the main task can both pass. The skills cover what the checker can't see.

A project's own content guide, design system or spacing tokens win over the skills.

### Rendering

`ui-standards render FILE|URL` opens a page in headless Chrome or Chromium. It saves screenshots at 1280 and 375px wide and checks the layout at 320px:

| Rule | Tier | Flags |
|---|---|---|
| `overflow-x` | Problem | The page scrolls sideways at 320px |
| `text-overlap` | Problem | Text overlapping other text |
| `hidden-visible` | Problem | An element marked `hidden` that still shows |
| `nested-card`, `single-control-card`, `multiple-primary` | Problem | The same rules, measured on the rendered page, including markup built at runtime |
| `small-target` | Advice | A click target under 24px with no clear space around it |
| `long-lines` | Advice | Text lines over 80 characters |

The checker talks to Chrome over its debugging pipe, so nothing else needs installing. Rendering isn't required. The ui-layout skill tells the agent when a render is worth it: after building a screen or changing its structure, once per kind of page.

## Install

All three agents need `python3` 3.9 or later on your PATH. Rendering also needs Chrome or Chromium.

### Claude Code

Run these in Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add tavonkelly/claude-ui
/plugin install ui-standards@claude-ui
```

On Claude Code 2.1.275 or later, one command does both:

```
/plugin install ui-standards --marketplace tavonkelly/claude-ui
```

Start a new session to load it. The plugin installs both skills and all four hooks, so there is nothing else to set up.

### Claude Code without the plugin

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tavonkelly/claude-ui.git
```

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills && cp -R claude-ui/skills/ui-text claude-ui/skills/ui-layout ~/.claude/skills/
```

Then add this `hooks` block to `~/.claude/settings.json`. If the file already has a `hooks` block, add each entry to the matching list.

```json
"hooks": {
  "SessionStart": [{"hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "python3 \"$HOME/.claude/skills/ui-text/bin/ui-standards\" hook session", "timeout": 10}]}],
  "PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "python3 \"$HOME/.claude/skills/ui-text/bin/ui-standards\" hook pre", "timeout": 10}]}],
  "PostToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "python3 \"$HOME/.claude/skills/ui-text/bin/ui-standards\" hook post", "timeout": 15}]}],
  "Stop": [{"hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "python3 \"$HOME/.claude/skills/ui-text/bin/ui-standards\" hook stop", "timeout": 15}]}]
}
```

### Codex

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tavonkelly/claude-ui.git
```

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.codex/skills && cp -R claude-ui/skills/ui-text claude-ui/skills/ui-layout ~/.codex/skills/
```

If you don't have a `~/.codex/hooks.json` yet, copy the one in this repo:

If you already have one, add the four entries from `codex/hooks.json` to it. Then start Codex, run `/hooks` and trust the new hooks. Codex skips a hook until you trust it, and again each time it changes.

Codex sends file edits as `apply_patch` text, and the checker reads the patch to find which files and lines changed. The Codex hooks are tested with sample payloads in each shape Codex has used for edits, not yet in a live Codex session. If they don't fire for you, please open an issue with your Codex version.

### opencode

```bash

```


Then add the rules below to `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`. opencode has no hook for the end of a turn, so flags appear only in each edit's result. ### The rules

The session hook adds these rules in Claude Code and Codex. Without hooks, or in opencode, add them to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` or `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
## UI text

Text on a screen is not prose. Name the thing or the action in a few words, show state as state, and keep explanations of how the system works off the screen. Before writing or changing any text a product's user sees, load the ui-text skill.

## UI layout

A screen has one job and one primary action. Put what users need first, group with space before boxes, don't nest cards, and keep internals in a developer view. Before building or rearranging a screen, load the ui-layout skill.
```

### Upgrading from 1.x

Version 1 was a plugin named `ui-text` in a repo named `claude-ui-text`. GitHub redirects the old URL, but the plugin and marketplace names changed, so remove the old plugin first:

```
/plugin uninstall ui-text@claude-ui-text
/plugin marketplace remove claude-ui-text
```

Then install as above. For a manual install, copy both skill folders again. Hooks that still call `bin/ui-text` keep working, because that file now runs `ui-standards`.

## Commands

```
ui-standards check PATH... [--ignore-rule RULE] [--only GLOB] [--json]
ui-standards render FILE|URL [--out DIR] [--wait MS] [--session ID]
ui-standards flags
ui-standards waive ID [ID...] --reason TEXT
ui-standards selftest
```

`check` reads whole files or folders, text and layout together, and exits with 1 when it finds problems, so it also works in CI. Advice doesn't change the exit code.

```bash
python3 skills/ui-text/bin/ui-standards check src/
```

There are no inline ignore comments and no ignored folders. To skip a rule for one run, pass `--ignore-rule`.

Flags and waivers last for one session. The checker keeps them in `~/.cache/ui-standards`, outside your repos. Render screenshots go to `.ui-standards/render` in the folder you run it from, so the agent can open them; that folder has its own `.gitignore`, so git skips it. Set `UI_STANDARDS_STATE` to keep them somewhere else. The checker makes no network calls. A render opens only the page you give it, plus whatever that page loads itself.

## Updating

For the plugin, run `/plugin marketplace update claude-ui` in Claude Code. For a manual install, run `git pull` in your clone and copy the files again.

## Sources

The text standard draws on the GOV.UK Service Manual (writing for user interfaces), the Microsoft Win32 UI text guide and Writing Style Guide, Apple's Human Interface Guidelines (Writing, Buttons, Alerts), Material 3 content design, and the content guidelines from Shopify, Atlassian and Mailchimp.

The layout standard draws on Nielsen Norman Group research on visual hierarchy, scanning patterns, proximity, common region, cards, progressive disclosure, empty states, dashboards and form design; the GOV.UK Design System; Apple's Human Interface Guidelines (Layout, Buttons); Material 3 layout and cards; Microsoft Fluent 2; IBM Carbon; Shopify Polaris; Atlassian Design; GitHub Primer; Refactoring UI; and Stephen Few on dashboard design. Several landing-page checks follow rules in [impeccable](https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable) and [design-slop-cop](https://github.com/AdrianKrebs/design-slop-cop).

Both use WCAG 2.2 and ISO 9241-110, 9241-112 and 9241-125. Where sources disagree, the skills pick one default and state it, so the agent doesn't have to choose.
